steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring React and useState into your file.
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported and available for use.
successCriteria: The import statement correctly imports both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state in your components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement isn't quite complete. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package using the correct syntax.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns null for now. Use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Define a component that returns null. This will be the main entry point for your application.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: The code should contain a component named App that returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the main App component. Returning null for now is fine - we'll add content in later steps.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've created a component named App that returns null. Check that you've used the correct component name and return statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't properly defined. Create a functional component named App that returns null.

steps.title: Define the initial state interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface called 'State' with a single property 'count' of type 'number'.
steps.hint: Create an interface using the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definition.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a TypeScript interface that defines the shape of your application state.
successCriteria: The code should include an interface named 'State' with a 'count' property typed as 'number'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the State interface with the correct type for the count property.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've defined an interface named 'State' with a 'count' property of type 'number'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to create a TypeScript interface called 'State' with a 'count' property of type 'number'.

steps.title: Initialize the application state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use useState with the State interface to initialize a state variable with an initial value of { count: 0 }.
steps.hint: Call useState with the initial object and destructure the returned array to get the state variable and setter function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now has a state variable initialized with { count: 0 } using the State interface for type safety.
successCriteria: useState hook is called inside App component
State interface is used as generic type for useState
State variable and setter are properly destructured
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully initialized the application state with proper TypeScript typing. The useState hook now provides type-safe access to your count state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there are a few issues. Make sure you're using the State interface as the generic type for useState, and that you're destructuring both the state variable and setter function from the useState return value.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's review: Inside the App component, you need to call useState with the State interface as the generic type and { count: 0 } as the initial value. Remember to destructure the returned array into a state variable and setter function.

steps.title: Create the reducer function
steps.instruction: Create a reducer function named 'reducer' that takes the current state and an action as parameters, and returns a new state based on the action type. Place this function inside your App component (above the return statement).
steps.hint: Define a function with two parameters: 'state' of type 'State' and 'action' with a 'type' property. Use a switch statement on action.type to handle different actions.
steps.expectedOutcome: A reducer function is defined inside the App component that can handle state updates based on action types.
successCriteria: The code should include a function named 'reducer' that takes 'state' and 'action' parameters, uses a switch statement on action.type, and returns a new State object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a reducer function that follows the Redux pattern for state updates.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your reducer function has the correct signature (state: State, action: { type: string }) and returns a State object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The reducer function is missing or doesn't match the expected pattern. Remember to create a function named 'reducer' that handles state updates based on action types.

steps.title: Define action types
steps.instruction: Define TypeScript types for your Redux-style actions. Create a union type called 'Action' that can be either an INCREMENT or DECREMENT action, each with a 'type' property.
steps.hint: Use a discriminated union with literal string types for 'type'. For example: type Action = { type: 'INCREMENT' } | { type: 'DECREMENT' }
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have defined TypeScript types for your Redux actions, creating a union type 'Action' that describes both INCREMENT and DECREMENT action shapes.
successCriteria: The code should include a union type called 'Action' that combines at least two action types, each with a 'type' property using string literal types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined TypeScript action types. This creates a type-safe foundation for your reducer to handle different actions.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've created a proper union type for actions. Check that you have both INCREMENT and DECREMENT action types defined.
steps.feedbackWrong: The action types aren't defined correctly. You need to create TypeScript types for INCREMENT and DECREMENT actions, then combine them into a union type called 'Action'.

steps.title: Create action creator functions
steps.instruction: Create two action creator functions named 'increment' and 'decrement' that return properly typed action objects. Place them after the action types definition.
steps.hint: Action creators are simple functions that return action objects with a 'type' property. Use the action types you defined earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have two functions that return action objects with proper type properties.
successCriteria: The code must include both 'increment' and 'decrement' functions that return objects with a 'type' property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the action creator functions. These functions will help dispatch actions in a predictable way.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but you need both 'increment' and 'decrement' functions that return action objects with a 'type' property.
steps.feedbackWrong: Action creators should be simple functions that return action objects. Make sure you create both 'increment' and 'decrement' functions that return objects with a 'type' property.

steps.title: Create a dispatch function
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, create a dispatch function that takes an action object and updates the state by calling the reducer with the current state and the action.
steps.hint: Define a function inside the component that calls setState with the result of reducer(state, action).
steps.expectedOutcome: A dispatch function is defined inside the App component that will update the state using the reducer.
successCriteria: The code should include a dispatch function that takes an action parameter and calls setState with the result of reducer(state, action).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a dispatch function that will update the state using the reducer. This is a key part of the Redux pattern.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your dispatch function properly calls setState with the result of reducer(state, action).
steps.feedbackWrong: The dispatch function is missing or incorrect. It should take an action parameter and update state by calling setState(reducer(state, action)).

steps.title: Add the main container structure
steps.instruction: In the App component's return statement, wrap the existing content inside a div element with className 'app'.
steps.hint:
Add an opening
before the existing content and a closing
after it.
steps.expectedOutcome: The main content is now wrapped in a div with className 'app'.
successCriteria: The return statement should contain a div element with className 'app' that wraps the existing h1 element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wrapped the app content in a container div with the correct className.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a container, but check if it has className 'app' and properly wraps the h1 element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The main container structure is not correct. Make sure to wrap the existing content in a div with className 'app'.

steps.title: Display the current count
steps.instruction: Inside the main container div, add a heading element that displays the current count value from your state.
steps.hint: Use JSX curly braces to embed the state.count value inside an <h2> or similar heading element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show the current count value (initially 0) below the main title.
successCriteria: Add a heading element (e.g., <h2>) inside the container div that displays the value of state.count using JSX interpolation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully displayed the current count from state in the UI. This shows how state data can be rendered in React components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're displaying the actual count value from state (state.count) inside the heading element using JSX curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: The count isn't being displayed correctly. You need to add a heading element that shows the value of state.count from your useState hook.

steps.title: Add increment button and wire to dispatch
steps.instruction: Add a button element inside the main container that displays 'Increment' and has an onClick handler that calls the dispatch function with an increment action.
steps.hint: Create a button with text content 'Increment' and an onClick attribute that calls dispatch with an action object containing type: 'INCREMENT'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a button that dispatches an action
<button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'INCREMENT' })}>
  Increment
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Increment' appears in the UI that, when clicked, will eventually trigger the increment action through the dispatch function.
successCriteria: Action object with type: 'INCREMENT' passed to dispatch
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added an increment button wired to dispatch the increment action.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your button has the correct text and an onClick handler that calls dispatch with { type: 'INCREMENT' }.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not properly configured. Check that you've added a button element with 'Increment' text and an onClick handler that dispatches the increment action.

steps.title: Add decrement button and wire to dispatch
steps.instruction: Add a button element inside the main container that, when clicked, dispatches a decrement action. The button should have the text 'Decrement' and call dispatch with an action object that has type: 'DECREMENT'.
steps.hint: Add a <button> element after the increment button. Use onClick to call dispatch with { type: 'DECREMENT' }.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a button that dispatches an action
<button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'DECREMENT' })}>
  Decrement
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A 'Decrement' button appears next to the 'Increment' button. Clicking it decreases the displayed count by 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the decrement button and wired it to dispatch the DECREMENT action. This completes the basic Redux pattern with two action types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you have a button with 'Decrement' text and an onClick that calls dispatch with { type: 'DECREMENT' }.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Add a button element with the text 'Decrement' and an onClick handler that calls dispatch with an action object { type: 'DECREMENT' }.
